title: “And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable,…
content: “And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, Mahānāma, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure – that is the gratification of sensual pleasures.”

title: Elder Nisabha: Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, Those things so agreeable, Which delight the mind — With faith, I went forth, Putting…
content:
Elder Nisabha:

Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
Those things so agreeable,
Which delight the mind —
With faith, I went forth,
Putting an end to suffering.

I do not delight in death,
I do not delight in life.
I await the time,
Mindful and clearly comprehending.

title: “And what, monks, are the things that should be fully understood? Form, monks, is a thing that should be fully understood; feeling … perception ……
content: “And what, monks, are the things that should be fully understood? Form, monks, is a thing that should be fully understood; feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is a thing that should be fully understood. These, monks, are the things that should be fully understood. And what, monks, is full understanding? The destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion — this, monks, is called full understanding.”

title: “Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, just a skeleton…
content:
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms. Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s body thrown in the charnel ground, just a skeleton with white bones like a shell … bones more than a year old … rotting bones reduced to powder. What do you think, monks? Has the former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?”
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Monks, such is the peril in the case of forms.”

title: “Householder, suppose a man carries a blazing grass torch against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go…
content: “Householder, suppose a man carries a blazing grass torch against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go of that blazing torch, could it burn his hand, his arm, or some part of his body, and would he thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

title: “Good sirs, if a monk, reflecting, knows: ‘I dwell much with a greedy mind; I dwell much with a hateful mind; I dwell much with…
content: “Good sirs, if a monk, reflecting, knows: ‘I dwell much with a greedy mind; I dwell much with a hateful mind; I dwell much with a mind overcome by sloth and torpor; I dwell much with restlessness; I dwell much with doubt; I dwell much with anger; I dwell much with a defiled mind; I dwell much with bodily fever; I dwell much with laziness; I dwell much with an unconcentrated mind’ — then that monk should make a strong wish, arouse effort, be energetic, strive, be strong-minded, not fall away, be mindful and clearly comprehending for the abandonment of those evil, unwholesome states. Just as, good sirs, if a turban or head were on fire, one would make a strong wish, arouse effort, be energetic, strive, be strong-minded, not fall away, be mindful and clearly comprehending to extinguish that turban or head — so too, that monk should make a strong wish … for the abandonment of those evil, unwholesome states. If a monk, reflecting, knows: ‘I dwell much with a mind free from greed; I dwell much with a mind free from hatred; I dwell much with a mind free from sloth and torpor; I dwell much with a mind free from restlessness; I dwell much with a mind that has overcome doubt; I dwell much with a mind free from anger; I dwell much with an undefiled mind; I dwell much with a body free from fever; I dwell much with an energetic, striving mind; I dwell much with a concentrated mind’ — then that monk, established in those wholesome states, should further devote himself to the destruction of the defilements.”

title: “Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered, Seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Suffering is birth again and again.” “O…
content:
“Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered,
Seeking but not finding the builder of this house.
Suffering is birth again and again.”

“O house-builder, you are seen!
You shall not build a house again.
All your rafters are broken,
Your ridge-pole is shattered.
My mind has attained the unconditioned,
And the extinction of craving has been reached.”

title: “‘For life, the arahants have abandoned unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. Today, this night and day,…
content: “‘For life, the arahants have abandoned unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. Today, this night and day, I too abandon unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. In this factor, I follow the arahants and will observe the uposatha day.’”

title: - What hangs up the world? What envelops the world? What closes in the world? Upon what does the world stand? - Craving hangs up…
content:
- What hangs up the world?
What envelops the world?
What closes in the world?
Upon what does the world stand?
- Craving hangs up the world,
Aging envelops the world,
Death closes in the world,
Upon suffering the world stands.

title: “Here, venerable sir, a person has no stain but does not truly know: ‘There is no stain in me.’ For such a person, it can…
content: “Here, venerable sir, a person has no stain but does not truly know: ‘There is no stain in me.’ For such a person, it can be expected: ‘He will attend to the sign of the beautiful. By attending to the sign of the beautiful, greed will pollute his mind. He will die with greed, with ill-will, with delusion, with stain, his mind polluted.’ Venerable sir, just as a bronze bowl brought from the market or from the smithy, clean and pure, and the owner does not use it, does not wipe it, and throws it into a dusty place – that bowl, after a time, becomes more defiled and dustier.”
